content: Sichuan pepper, also known as Szechuan pepper, is the outer husk of the small fruit produced by various species in the genus Zanthoxylum, most commonly Z. piperitum, Z. simulans, Z. sancho, and Z. schinifolium. It is widely cultivated and consumed as a spice in Asia. Despite its name, it is not related to black pepper (Piper nigrum) or chili peppers (Capsicum species). This spice is a key ingredient in Sichuan cuisine from China, as well as in Tibetan, Bhutanese, Nepalese, Japanese, and Konkani cuisines, among others. In Chinese, it is called huā jiāo (花椒), meaning flower pepper, and less commonly shān jiāo (山椒), meaning mountain pepper. In Japanese, it is referred to as sanshō (山椒), using the same Chinese characters. In Konkani, it is known as tepal or tirphal. In the United States, it is sometimes sold under names like fagara or flower pepper. Sichuan pepper has a distinctive aroma and flavor that is not hot or pungent like black or white pepper or chili peppers. Instead, it has a slightly lemony fragrance and produces a tingling, numbing sensation in the mouth, which is attributed to its content of hydroxy-alpha-sanshool (approximately 3%). Culinary preparations often involve lightly toasting and crushing the husks before adding them to dishes, as only the husks are used while the seeds are discarded. It is typically added at the end of cooking. Sichuan pepper is often paired with star anise and ginger and is a prominent component of spicy Sichuan cuisine. It complements dishes made with fish, duck, chicken, and fried eggplant. When consumed in larger quantities, it has an alkaline pH and can cause a numbing effect on the lips. The combination of Sichuan pepper and chili pepper creates the characteristic flavor known as mala (麻辣), meaning numbing and spicy, which is a hallmark of Sichuan cooking. Sichuan pepper is also available as an oil, marketed as Sichuan pepper oil or Huajiao oil. This oil is particularly suited for stir-fried noodle dishes that do not include hot spices. A common recipe involves cooking noodles and vegetables with ginger oil and brown sugar, then adding rice vinegar and Sichuan pepper oil after cooking. Another preparation, hua jiao yan (花椒盐), is a mixture of roasted salt and Sichuan pepper, often served as a condiment with chicken, duck, or pork dishes. The peppercorns can also be lightly fried to create a spicy oil with versatile culinary applications. In the Himalayan regions, where few spices can be cultivated, Sichuan pepper is one of the essential spices in Tibetan and Bhutanese cuisine. It is used to flavor momo dumplings, which are filled with vegetables, cottage cheese, or minced yak meat, beef, or pork, and seasoned with Sichuan pepper, garlic, ginger, and onion. The dumplings are steamed and served dry with a spicy sauce. Tibetans believe that Sichuan pepper can sanitize less-than-fresh meat, though it may simply mask unpleasant flavors. In Japan, the dried and powdered leaves of Zanthoxylum sancho are used to add mild heat and fragrance to noodle dishes and soups. The fresh leaves, known as kinome (木の芽), are used to flavor vegetables, particularly bamboo shoots, and to garnish soups. Other parts of the plant, including buds, seeds, flowers, and hulls, are also utilized. Sichuan peppercorns are a traditional ingredient in Chinese five-spice powder and the Japanese seasoning shichimi togarashi (seven-flavor spice). In Korean cuisine, two species, Z. piperitum and Z. schinifolium, are used. The chemical composition of various Zanthoxylum species varies. For example, Z. fagara (found in Central and Southern Africa and South America) contains alkaloids and coumarins. Z. simulans (from Taiwan) is rich in beta-myrcene, limonene, 1,8-cineole, and Z-beta-ocimene. Z. armatum (from Nepal) contains linalool (50%), limonene, methyl cinnamate, and cineole. Z. rhetsa is characterized by sabinene, limonene, pinenes, para-cymene, terpenes, 4-terpineol, and alpha-terpineol. Z. sancho (from Japan) contains citronellal, citronellol, and Z-3-hexenal. The genus name Zanthoxylum derives from the Greek words xanthos (blond) and xylon (wood), meaning blond wood. From 1968 to 2005, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) banned the importation of Sichuan peppercorns due to their potential to carry citrus canker, as the plant belongs to the same family (Rutaceae) as citrus trees. This was not a concern for human consumption but rather for agricultural safety. The ban was loosely enforced until 2002 and was lifted in 2005, provided the peppercorns were heat-treated to approximately 70°C (160°F) to eliminate the bacteria before importation. Sichuan pepper is known by various names, including Szechwan pepper, Chinese pepper, Japanese pepper, aniseed pepper, prickly ash, fagara, sansho, Nepal pepper, and Indonesian lemon pepper. In Tibet, it is called e-ma or Kham pepper. In Nepal, where it is extensively used, it is known as timur (Z. alatum). In the Indian states of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Goa, it is called teppal or tirphal (Z. rhetsa). The fresh fruits, which grow in clusters like grapes on thorny trees, are green and used as a flavoring agent in curries made with coconut, chilies, and other spices. The fruits are seasonal, available during the monsoon period. When dried, the fruit's flesh hardens, turns brownish-black, and opens to reveal black seeds, which are discarded. The dried fruit is stored for year-round use, primarily in fish preparations and some vegetarian dishes. The spice has a strong woody aroma and is typically removed before eating the curry. The tree is also known as jummn kayee or gamathe haralu in Kannada and koili kaya in Malayalam.
